inline.s: The ālaya and the mental, together joined, make the red and white to grow.
The arbuda and the peshi, from defiled karma born in many ways;
The karma-wind swells the four great elements, and birth comes forth as fruit that ripens.
Five and five and five, and nine kinds of sores and apertures;
With nails and teeth and hair complete, when all is full, then birth takes place.
The newborn is a worm in dung, and like a man awakening from sleep;
The eyes open and see forms, and discrimination gradually grows.
When discrimination has been decided through, the lips and palate join and meet;
Then speech begins to issue forth, just like a parrot and the rest.
Following the dispositions of all beings, one establishes them in the Great Vehicle;
That is no ground for evil views; the sectarians cannot accept it.”
“The vehicle realized within oneself is no range for reckoning thought;
Pray tell: after the Buddha’s passing, who will be able to uphold it?”
“Mahāmati, you should know that after the Sugata’s nirvāṇa,
In future ages there will be those who hold to my Dharma.
In the land of South India a bhikshu of great renown and virtue;
His name is Nāgārjuna, who will shatter the schools of being and non-being.
He will make known in the world my Supreme Great Vehicle;
He will attain the first Ground of Joy and be reborn in the Land of Bliss.
Things arising from conditions: neither being nor non-being is tenable;
In conditions the fool imagines a thing, and discriminates being and non-being;
Views such as these of the sectarians stand far apart from my Dharma.
The names of all dharmas ever follow upon their place of birth;
Both what has been habituated and what is now habituated, each turns and discriminates with the other;
If one does not speak of names, the whole world would be bewildered;
To dispel bewilderment, therefore, names and words are established.
The foolish discriminate all dharmas, deluded by names and words;
And so too the conditioned arising of all things: these are the three kinds of discrimination.
Because it neither arises nor ceases, its own nature is like space;
Its self-nature is nothing at all: this is called the mark of vain imagining.
Like illusion, shadow, mirage, mirror-image, dream, and fire-wheel;
Like echo and like a phantom city: this is the dependent arising.
Suchness, emptiness, non-duality, the real limit, and the dharma-nature;
All of these are free of discrimination: this I call the perfected nature.
The range of language and of mental factors falls falsely into the two extremes;
Wisdom discriminates the ultimate truth; that wisdom is free of discrimination.
To the wise it appears, to the foolish it appears not;
Thus what wisdom reveals: all dharmas are without marks.
Like a necklace of counterfeit gold, not gold, yet the fool calls it gold;
So too are all dharmas: the sectarians vainly reckon and measure.
All dharmas have no beginning and no end, abiding in the mark of the real;
The whole world is uncreated: the vainly imagining cannot comprehend it.
Whatever dharmas there were in the past, and in the future and the present;
All dharmas such as these are entirely unborn.
Because conditions come together, therefore things are spoken of as existing;
If one is free of that coming-together, there is no arising and no ceasing.
But in dharmas arisen from conditions, neither sameness nor difference can be found;
Spoken of briefly, they are arising; spoken of at length, they are cessation.
The one is the emptiness of the unborn, and the other is the emptiness of the born;
The emptiness of the unborn is supreme; the emptiness of the born is decay and ruin.
The various bodies born of the will, I say, are merely different names.
With regard to all the sutras, vinayas, and treatises, a pure discrimination is stirred up;
If one does not understand selflessness, one relies on the teaching and not on the meaning,
And beings vainly discriminate, seeing what is like a hare’s horn,
Discrimination itself is delusion, like a thirsty beast pursuing a mirage.
Through false attachment and grasping, discrimination is stirred up;
If one is free of the cause of false grasping, discrimination does not arise.
The profound and vast and wide: to know the sovereign freedom of all lands;
I speak this for the Buddha’s sons, and not for the śrāvakas.
The three existences are empty and impermanent, far removed from self and what belongs to self;
For the śrāvakas I speak in just these general terms.
Not clinging to any dharma, dwelling alone in still quiescence;
Thinking on the fruit of the pratyekabuddha, I speak thus for those beings.
The body is dependent arising, yet delusion does not see itself;
It discriminates an outer self-nature, and so makes the mind falsely arise.
The fruit of karmic reward, empowerment, and the births of every kind of realm;
And what is obtained in dreams: these are the four natures of the superknowledges.
What is obtained within a dream, and by the Buddha’s awesome power;
The births of every kind of realm and the rest are not the superknowledge of karmic reward.
Habitual tendencies perfuming the mind bring forth appearances like things;
The common and foolish cannot awaken to this, and so it is spoken of as arising.
Following along with vain discrimination, how long do outer marks endure?
For just so long delusion grows, and one does not see that one’s own mind is deluded.”
“Why is it taught that there is arising, and not that there is what is seen?
Seeing without anything seen, for whom and how could it be taught?”
“The essence of mind is itself originally pure, though joined with the mental and all the consciousnesses;
Because habitual tendencies ever perfume it, it becomes all manner of turbidity and confusion.
The storehouse consciousness abandons the body, and the mental seeks the various realms;
Consciousness is deluded into seeming objects, and having seen them, grasps them with greed.
What is seen is only one’s own mind; no outer object can be found;
If one cultivates such contemplation, one casts off vain thinking and accords with suchness.
The range of those in samādhi, of karma, and of the Buddha’s awesome power;
These three are inconceivable, the range of the inconceivable wisdom.
The past and future pudgala, space, and nirvāṇa;
I follow the conventions of the world; the ultimate truth is free of letters.
The two vehicles and the sectarians alike rely upon and rest in views;
Deluded about mind-only, they vainly discriminate outer objects.
The arhat and the pratyekabuddha, and the bodhi of the Buddhas;
The seed firmly accomplished: a Buddha appears in a dream and sprinkles them with water.”
“The illusion of mind tends toward stillness: why is being and non-being spoken of?
Where, and for whom? For what reason? Pray explain it for us.”
“Because of delusion about mind-only, being and non-being are spoken of as illusion;
Arising and ceasing answer to one another, and mark and marked are equal.
Discrimination is called the mental consciousness, together with the five consciousnesses;
Like images and a torrent, they arise from the seeds of the mind.
If the mind and the mental, and all the consciousnesses, do not arise;
Then one attains the body born of the will, and also reaches the Buddha-ground.
The various conditions, the skandhas, and the realms, and the own-marks of person and dharmas;
Are all mere mind-made designations, like a dream and a hair-net.
Seeing the world as illusion and dream, one rests upon the real;
The real is free of all marks, and free too of corresponding causes.
What the noble ones realize within, ever dwelling in no-thought;
Delusion answers to causes, and so grasps the world as real.
When all vain talk is extinguished, delusion then does not arise;
Wherever there is deluded discrimination, a foolish mind ever keeps appearing.
All dharmas are empty and without nature, and yet are ever and not ever;
This is the view of those who propound arising, not the doctrine of the unborn.
Sameness, difference, both, and neither; nature and sovereign lord;
Time, atoms, and primal matter: conditions discriminating the world.
Consciousness is the seed of birth and death; because there is a seed, there is birth;
As a painting depends upon the wall, so when one understands, it at once ceases.
Just as one sees an illusory man, and there is illusory birth and death;
So too are the common and foolish: through delusion bondage and release arise.
The two kinds of dharmas, inner and outer, and their conditions;
The practitioner observes, and they all abide in signlessness.
Habitual tendencies do not leave the mind, nor do they dwell together with it;
Though the mind is entwined by habit, the mind’s mark has no distinction.
The mind is like a white garment; the habits of consciousness are the grime;
Soiled by the stains of habit, they keep the mind from showing forth.
I say it is like space: neither existing nor non-existing;
